rules: Every class ends with a thirty second memo: one takeaway and one link to your real work.
Leadership is a behavior, not a position.

sessions.title: Leader as architect
sessions.idea: Leaders shape behavior twice: directly, by what they do, and indirectly, by what they build around people.

readings.idea: A leader is also a designer. The setting you build keeps working when you are not in the room.
points: Most of what people do at work is shaped by the setting they work in, not by direct orders.
So a big part of leading is designing that setting on purpose: structure, systems, culture and the people you put in roles.
Good design makes the right behavior the easy behavior.

readings.idea: Management copes with complexity. Leadership copes with change. Organizations need both.
points: Planning and budgeting is management. Setting a direction is leadership.
Organizing and staffing is management. Aligning people behind the direction is leadership.
Controlling and problem solving is management. Motivating and inspiring is leadership.
Most companies are overmanaged and underled, but strong leadership with weak management is no better.

checks.q: Setting a direction is to leadership as ______ is to management.
checks.why: Kotter pairs them: direction with planning, aligning with organizing, inspiring with controlling.

checks.q: Kotter says most companies are
checks.why: He also warns that strong leadership with weak management is no better.

checks.q: Leader as architect means
o: Shaping behavior through the setting you design
checks.why: Structure, systems, culture and people keep shaping behavior after you leave the room.

prompts: Where have you seen a well-designed setting make good behavior easy?
When did a team you were on have strong management and weak leadership, or the reverse?

sessions.title: Leading by doing
sessions.idea: What separates strong leaders is less IQ or skill than emotional intelligence, and the safety they create for others to speak.

readings.idea: Emotional intelligence is the threshold that separates star leaders from the rest, and it can be learned.
points: Five components: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skill.
The first three are about managing yourself. The last two are about managing relationships.
It can be learned, but slowly, through practice and feedback, not a seminar.

checks.q: Which Goleman component includes comfort with ambiguity and openness to change?
checks.why: Self-regulation is control of impulses and moods, which shows up as integrity and comfort with ambiguity.

checks.q: Psychological safety is
o: A shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk
checks.why: Edmondson pairs it with high standards. Safety without standards is a comfort zone.

checks.q: Persuasiveness and building teams are hallmarks of
checks.why: Social skill is friendliness with a purpose: moving people in the direction you want.

prompts: Which of the five components is strongest for you, and which do others see differently?
What does a leader do in the first five minutes of a meeting that makes it safe to disagree?

sessions.title: Leading through design
sessions.idea: There is no best structure, only a fit between structure, strategy, people and culture.

readings.t: Do You Have a Well-Designed Organization?
readings.idea: Run any design through nine tests: four on fit, five on good design.
points: Fit tests: market advantage, parenting advantage, people, and feasibility.
Good design tests: specialist cultures, difficult links, redundant hierarchy, accountability, and flexibility.
Most structures grow by politics and accident. The tests make design a deliberate choice.

readings.a: Nadler and Tushman, via Mercer Delta
readings.idea: Performance comes from fit between the work, the people, the formal organization and the informal culture.
points: Inputs (environment, resources, history) feed a strategy.
Four parts turn strategy into output: work, people, formal organization, informal organization.
The fit between parts matters more than any one part. A great engine in the wrong car still fails.

checks.q: A matrix structure trades simplicity for
o: The ability to manage two priorities at once
checks.why: Two reporting lines let you balance function and product, at the cost of clarity and speed.

checks.q: Which is a Goold and Campbell fit test?
checks.why: The four fit tests are market advantage, parenting advantage, people and feasibility.

checks.q: In the congruence model, the informal organization is
checks.why: Formal is the chart and systems. Informal is how things really get done.

prompts: If you designed your team from scratch tomorrow, what would you change first, and which test does it fail today?
Where is the informal organization doing work the formal one cannot?

sessions.title: Leadership through culture
sessions.idea: Culture is how people behave when no one is telling them what to do, and leaders can map it and shape it.

readings.t: The Leader’s Guide to Corporate Culture
readings.idea: Eight culture styles sit on two axes: how people interact, and how they respond to change.
points: Interaction runs from independent to interdependent. Response to change runs from flexible to stable.
The eight styles: caring, purpose, learning, enjoyment, results, authority, safety and order.
Styles next to each other on the map coexist easily. Styles far apart pull against each other.
Culture is shaped by what leaders say, what they reward, how they design the organization, and who they hire.

sessions.caseName: The Lego Group leadership playground, Part A
due: First third of semester feedback survey

checks.q: The two axes of the culture map are
o: People interactions and response to change
checks.why: Independent to interdependent, and flexible to stable.

checks.q: A culture built on planning, caution and preparedness is
checks.why: Safety sits on the stable end of the change axis.

checks.q: Which pair is most likely to clash?
checks.why: Learning is flexible and exploratory. Safety is stable and cautious. They sit far apart on the map.

prompts: Name the two styles that best describe your current team. Would your manager pick the same two?
What one behavior gets rewarded where you work that the stated values do not mention?

sessions.title: Influence and driving change
sessions.idea: Change fails at predictable steps, and persuasion is a process of learning and negotiating, not a pitch.

readings.t: Leading Change: Why Transformation Efforts Fail
readings.idea: Eight steps, in order. Skipping one creates the illusion of speed and never a good result.
points: Urgency, coalition, vision, communicate the vision, remove obstacles, short-term wins, consolidate, anchor in culture.
Each step has a matching error. Declaring victory too soon is one of the most common.
Communicating the vision is usually short by a factor of ten.

readings.idea: Persuasion works in four steps: credibility, common ground, vivid evidence and emotional connection.
points: Credibility comes from expertise and from relationships.
Frame the goal around what the audience already cares about.
Back the case with vivid stories and examples, not only numbers.
Read the audience’s emotions and match your intensity to theirs.
Common mistakes: the hard sell, refusing to compromise, assuming argument alone wins, and treating it as one shot.

checks.q: Kotter’s first step is
checks.why: Without urgency, the rest never gets enough energy.

checks.q: Conger’s first step in persuasion is
checks.why: Expertise and relationships come first; the audience has to trust the messenger.

checks.q: Declaring victory too soon breaks which Kotter step?
o: Consolidate gains and produce more change
checks.why: Step 7. Celebrate wins, but keep the change going until it is anchored.

prompts: Think of a change at work that stalled. Which of Kotter’s steps was skipped?
Who do you have to persuade without authority, and what is your credibility with them built on?

sessions.title: Teaming
sessions.idea: Team leaders manage tensions that never fully resolve, and they decide which conflict to encourage and which to defuse.

readings.idea: Leading a team means managing ongoing tensions, not solving them once.
points: Unity and diversity: enough shared identity to act together, enough difference to think well.
Support and confrontation: back people, and challenge them.
Performance and learning: deliver now, and build the team’s capacity for later.
Leader authority and team discretion: when to decide, and when to let the team decide.

sessions.caseName: (Re)building a Global Team: Tariq Khan at Tek

checks.q: Which conflict type usually helps a team?
o: Process conflict over who does what
checks.why: Debate over ideas improves decisions. Personal friction usually hurts them.

checks.q: Adding one person to a team of 6 adds how many new communication links?
checks.why: Links are n(n-1)/2. Six people have 15, seven have 21, so the new person adds 6.

checks.q: Hill’s support versus confrontation tension means
o: Choose between being liked and being respected
checks.why: Both are needed. The skill is the mix and the timing.

prompts: Which of Hill’s tensions do you lean too far on?
How would you rebuild trust on a team that has never met in person?

sessions.title: Navigating conflict
sessions.idea: Hot conflicts are about meaning and identity, not data, so more analysis rarely ends them. Slowing down and inquiring does.

readings.t: Too Hot to Handle? How to Manage Relationship Conflict
readings.a: Amy Edmondson and Diana McLain Smith
readings.idea: Cool conflicts yield to data. Hot ones yield to examining your own reasoning and asking about theirs.
points: Cool conflicts are about facts and can be settled by analysis.
Hot conflicts involve values, interests and identity. Each side reads the same facts differently.
Leaders first notice their own reactions and the story they are telling themselves.
Then they share their reasoning and ask about the other person’s, before arguing for a position.

checks.q: A conflict over whose values the strategy reflects is
checks.why: When identity and values are involved, more data rarely settles it.

checks.q: The first move in a hot conflict is
o: Notice your own reaction and story
checks.why: You cannot inquire well into theirs until you see your own.

checks.q: Inquiry means
o: Asking how the other person sees it and why
checks.why: Pair advocacy with inquiry: share your reasoning, then ask about theirs.

prompts: Think of a disagreement that kept coming back. Was it hot or cool?
What story were you telling yourself about the other person?

sessions.title: Collaborative decision making
sessions.idea: You cannot see your own biases, but you can spot them in the team that brings you a recommendation.

readings.t: Before You Make That Big Decision
readings.idea: Twelve questions a decision maker asks to catch bias in a team’s recommendation.
points: Ask about the team: self-interest, falling in love with the idea, groupthink.
Ask about the proposal: misleading analogies, missing alternatives, missing data, anchors, halo effect, sunk costs.
Ask about the assessment: an optimistic base case, a worst case that is not bad enough, too much caution.

checks.why: An early number pulls every later estimate toward it.

checks.q: “Is the worst case bad enough?” checks for
checks.why: Teams often set the worst case too close to the base case.

checks.q: A team attached to a past investment shows
checks.why: Money already spent should not drive the next decision.

prompts: Run your last big decision through the twelve questions. Which one stings?
When did hidden information in a group never get shared?

sessions.title: Leading by listening
sessions.idea: The biggest barrier to communication is the urge to judge, and people overestimate how clearly their own message lands.

readings.a: Carl R. Rogers and F. J. Roethlisberger
readings.idea: Listen with understanding: restate the other person’s view to their satisfaction before you reply.
points: The main barrier is our tendency to evaluate what we hear, right away, from our own frame.
The gateway is listening to understand the other person’s frame, not to rebut it.
A simple rule: before you speak, summarize what they said until they agree you got it.
Doing this takes courage, because you may be changed by what you hear.

videos: Communication and the illusion of transparency
due: Lab reflection, if you shared on Nov 5

checks.q: Rogers says the main barrier to communication is
o: The urge to evaluate and judge
checks.why: We judge from our frame before understanding theirs.

checks.q: In the tapping study, tappers expected listeners to name about half the songs. Listeners got
checks.why: About 2.5%. The tapper hears the melody in their head. The listener hears knocks.

checks.q: The illusion of transparency is
o: Believing others can read your thoughts and feelings more than they can
checks.why: It is why a message that feels obvious to you can land as noise.

prompts: When did you think you were clear and found out you were not?
In your next one on one, restate before you reply. What changed?

sessions.title: Motivating yourself and others
sessions.idea: Money matters, but less and more strangely than most managers assume. Autonomy, mastery and meaning do a lot of the work.

readings.t: Do Financial Incentives Drive Company Performance?
readings.src: Hard Facts, Dangerous Half-Truths, and Total Nonsense, ch. 5
readings.idea: Incentives work, sometimes too well. They get you exactly what you pay for, including the gaming.
points: Financial incentives do change behavior, so design them carefully.
They can crowd out intrinsic motivation and teamwork, and they invite gaming of the measure.
Pay is also a signal of what the organization values.
Evidence beats belief: test incentive schemes rather than assume they work.

checks.q: In Herzberg’s model, salary is a
checks.why: Fixing hygiene removes dissatisfaction but does not create motivation.

checks.q: In expectancy theory, motivation is zero if
o: Any one of expectancy, instrumentality or valence is zero
checks.why: It is a product. One zero sinks it.

checks.q: Which job characteristic multiplies the whole score?
checks.why: Motivating potential = average of variety, identity and significance, times autonomy, times feedback.

prompts: What motivates you that would not show up in a pay review?
Where have you seen an incentive get people to hit the number and miss the point?

sessions.title: Feedback
sessions.idea: Most feedback fails because the giver states conclusions, not data. Walk down the ladder of inference before you speak.

readings.a: Mark D. Cannon and Robert Witherspoon
readings.idea: Feedback is actionable when it leads to learning and results. Most of it attacks the person and stays vague.
points: Five flaws: attacks the person, vague, no examples, no range of application, no clear impact or next step.
Givers climb the ladder of inference from data to conclusions without noticing.
Self-serving bias in receivers and actor-observer bias in givers make each side see the other as the problem.
In a review of studies, 38% of feedback cases made performance worse.
Fix: ask yourself for examples, conditions, impact and the change you want. Use I statements.

sessions.caseName: Rob Parson at Morgan Stanley, Part A

checks.q: “Phil is a poor manager” fails mainly because it
o: Attacks the person and gives no example
checks.why: It names a trait, not a behavior, with no illustration or impact.

checks.q: The bottom rung of the ladder of inference is
checks.why: Then select data, paraphrase, name, explain, decide.

checks.q: In the Kluger and DeNisi review, feedback hurt performance in about
checks.why: Feedback that focuses on the self rather than the task often backfires.

prompts: Take a piece of feedback you gave recently. Which of the five flaws does it have?
What questions can you ask when someone gives you vague feedback?

sessions.title: Integrating it all
sessions.idea: Time is fixed. Energy is renewable. Leaders who manage energy across body, emotions, mind and purpose sustain performance.

readings.t: Manage Your Energy, Not Your Time
readings.idea: Four sources of energy, each renewed by small rituals.
points: Physical: sleep, movement, and breaks every 90 to 120 minutes.
Emotional: notice the story you tell, and look at it through other lenses.
Mental: protect focus. Do the most important task first, without email.
Spirit: spend time on what you do best, enjoy most and care about.

o: Time is finite but energy can be renewed
checks.why: Rituals renew energy, so the same hours produce more.

checks.why: It protects focus on the most important task.

checks.why: Reframing the story changes the feeling it produces.
